content: 1. The safety of levofloxacin (Lfx) in children was demonstrated to be extremely high, with only six children in the Lfx treatment group discontinuing therapy early due to adverse events (AEs), compared to one child in the placebo group. 2. The incidence of tuberculosis (TB) endpoints was lower than anticipated, and a significant proportion of children were excluded from the study due to presumptive TB. Additionally, the rate of interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA) positivity was lower than expected, with power calculations assuming a 40% positivity rate versus the observed 20%. 3. In the V-QUIN trial, Lfx was associated with a 45% reduction in microbiologically confirmed incident TB cases at 30 months. However, the low number of events led to wide confidence intervals in the primary analysis, which included the null value, indicating no statistical significance. 4. The incidence of grade 3–4 adverse events was low, with no significant differences observed between treatment groups. Furthermore, no acquired drug resistance to Lfx was detected. 5. Approximately three times as many co-prevalent TB cases were identified compared to incident TB cases. In a sub-study, microbiome diversity remained reduced six months after therapy, and there was an increase in nasal carriage of fluoroquinolone-resistant Staphylococcus aureus, a strain associated with higher virulence. 6. Two randomized trials, V-QUIN and TB CHAMP, completed in 2023, evaluated the safety, efficacy, and tolerability of six months of daily Lfx (6Lfx) as TB preventive treatment (TPT) for individuals exposed to multidrug-resistant or rifampicin-resistant TB (MDR/RR-TB). These trials aimed to inform the revision of the World Health Organization (WHO) TPT guidelines. 7. The systematic review updated prior data from 2016 to inform the 2018 WHO TPT guidelines and included studies on the efficacy, safety, tolerability, completion rates, acceptability, resource requirements, feasibility, cost-effectiveness, and equity impact of fluoroquinolone (FQ)-based TPT regimens for MDR/RR-TB contacts. 8. The review included studies with longitudinal designs (e.g., cohorts, case-control studies, case series, population-based observational studies), cost-effectiveness modeling, and randomized controlled trials (RCTs). Studies were required to report outcomes such as TB incidence, mortality, adverse events, treatment completion, emergence of FQ resistance, and acceptability. 9. Quality assessment of included studies was conducted independently by two reviewers using tools such as the Newcastle–Ottawa Scale, AXIS tool, and Joanna Briggs Institute critical appraisal tool. The GRADE framework was used to evaluate the quality of evidence. 10. Observational studies evaluating the efficacy of FQ-based TPT regimens showed no significant reduction in TB disease incidence. However, the studies were limited by small sample sizes and selection bias, leading to imprecise efficacy estimates. 11. In children, the safety of FQ-based TPT regimens was generally favorable, with low rates of serious adverse events and treatment discontinuation. However, higher rates of mild or moderate adverse events were observed in some studies, particularly when Lfx or moxifloxacin (Mfx) was combined with ethionamide (ETH) or ethambutol (EMB). 12. Among adults, the combination of Lfx and pyrazinamide (PZA) was poorly tolerated, with a significant proportion of participants discontinuing treatment due to drug-related adverse events. 13. Studies on the acceptability of FQ-based TPT regimens showed high levels of acceptance among caregivers and household contacts of MDR-TB patients, with approximately 80% agreeing to start treatment when offered. 14. Pharmacokinetic studies indicated that higher Lfx concentrations were associated with increased QT interval prolongation, but these effects diminished over time, and no cardiac adverse events were reported. 15. Overall, the review highlighted the need for further research to address gaps in evidence, particularly regarding the efficacy, safety, and feasibility of FQ-based TPT regimens in diverse populations and settings.
